To assess the validity of these predictions, we've calculated the semi-inclusive $R_{\ell}$ ratio for $b\to s\ell^+\ell^-$ transitions under lepton flavor non-conservation (LFNC) and compared it with the standard model (SM) prediction. Our results reveal that semi-inclusive $R_{\ell}$ ratios can be calculated with high precision using the weak effective couplings $V_{bs}^2$ and $V_{bs}^{\prime 2}$, which are directly related to $b\to s\ell^+\ell^-$ transition form factors. This finding enables precise predictions for $R_{\ell}$ ratios, including $R_{e}$, $R_{\mu}$, and $R_{\tau}$. Furthermore, by combining LFNC with muon-electron muon-nucleon scattering, we've derived constraints on LFNC parameters, specifically a lower bound on $\xi^\ell_{10}$ of 0.22 at the 90% confidence level. Additionally, in the presence of LFNC, lepton flavor non-conserving electric dipole moments (EDMs) can induce $R_{\ell}$ ratios, providing a connection between these two phenomena. To investigate this relationship, we've expressed the $\xi^\ell_{10}$ parameter in terms of lepton flavor non-conserving EDMS and $R_{\ell}$ ratios. Finally, in the context of a fourth-generation neutrino (type-I) left-handed neutrino (type-II) scenarios, we've derived expressions for $R_{\ell}$ ratios and established constraints on $\xi^\ell_{10}$ based on neutrino characteristics. These relationships are expected to be relevant for near-future experiments, including the Super tau factory. We introduce a novel approach for categorizing COVID-19 cases into two phases: suspecting and confirmed. Suspicious cases are individuals who have not contracted the virus but display symptoms, while confirmed cases are positive for COVID-19. Existing methods, however, treat all cases as having equal outcomes, neglecting the critical distinction between them. Building on BERT's token-level attributes, we propose a method that considers complementary semantic properties. We evaluate our approach's performance against a real-world Indian dataset and compare it to existing binary classification models. Notably, our approach surpasses BERT in accuracy, recall, and F1 score, while outperforming other baselines in F1 score and matching them in accuracy and recall. All experiment code and data will be made publicly available.

This modification yields three distinct dynamic regimes, characterized by different patterns of behavior. When changes are slow across all species, we see the emergence of sigmoidal trajectories. In contrast, if some species evolve quickly while others evolve slowly, the trajectories become complex and nonlinear, displaying sudden changes at "breakpoints." In this second regime, early-time behavior is dominated by the slowly evolving species, whereas at later times, the trajectories are influenced by the rapidly evolving species. Finally, when the differences in evolution speed are large, we see the appearance of "bifurcation points" where small fluctuations can suddenly lead to dramatic changes, resulting in drastically different outcomes. Our work builds on Ginzburg's theory, offering a more nuanced understanding of eco-evolutionary processes that acknowledges the diversity of time scales at play. By exploring the interplay between the lengths of these time scales, we gain insight into how eco-evolutionary processes have evolved over time, from geological periods to biological competition, potentially revealing new perspectives on this complex phenomenon. Our project, an ongoing effort led by the Quantum Computing and Quantum Simulation group from the University of Chicago, aims to establish a specialized platform at Fermilab for developing quantum computers.  A central aspect of this initiative is a platform we call the Fermilab Quantum Computing and Quantum Simulation (FCQS) system. Software developers frequently use incorrect cryptographic methods, which can compromise not only their own applications but also the security of related projects, due to the spread of inadequate practices through communities and resources. Existing research has examined programmer's use of cryptography in general, but it does not provide insights into how software engineers misuse cryptography in real-world scenarios. This study aims to change this by analyzing a large dataset of open-source Java/Python projects to identify how developers in these communities misuse cryptography in their code, which frequency and what level of experience versus inexperience are the primary drivers of these misuses. Our research found that Python, in particular, is more susceptible to misuses than Java, with a significant number of them related to reuse of security-related functions. However, the spread of inadequate practices within Python communities and the use of insecure libraries/patterns in popular projects contribute to this issue. Based on our research, we suggest several potential solutions to improve the security of Python projects, starting with the education of inexperience developers to recognize common misuses, the review of secure code snippets by experienced developers, the reporting of security vulnerabilities within popular projects, the avoidance of insecure libraries and the adoption of secure alternatives. Ultimately, a more secure future for Python projects will require collective efforts from the community to disseminate secure best practices. To address this challenge, we've developed a Proximal Mean Network called NuSPAN, capable of learning a sparse signal's characteristic behavior and effectively eliminating noise even when the signal's non-uniform pattern is unknown in advance. By representing the non-uniform pattern as a Gaussian distribution with an unknown mean and variance, NuSPAN's Gaussian-based proxy enables it to generalize to unseen patterns at test time. Through proximal regularization and an optimization process, NuSPAN's proxy converges to a tight shell around the true non-uniform pattern, allowing it to improve the quality of the sparse signal estimates on a sequence of tasks. To validate NuSPAN's performance, we applied it to a real-world seismic data inversion problem, where it successfully inverts multiple seismic data types by learning a common, sparse reflection pattern. Furthermore, we compared NuSPAN's performance to state-of-the-art sparse signal recovery methods, demonstrating its strong noise robustness and ability to generalize to unseen noise patterns at test time. To the best of our knowledge, NuSPAN is the first model to address non-uniform sparse signal recovery, representing a significant advancement in seismic data inversion and signal processing as a whole. Valuable historical documents, such as rare printed books and early manuscripts, are available for public use but suffer from inconsistent, often faulty, annotation practices. POS tagging in particular has received little attention from researchers, given the scarcity of large collections with existing labels. This study tackles the challenge of POS labeling in historical collections by adapting existing models to these texts. We found, however, that the task is better approached by training models to predict not just a single tag, but multiple possible sets of tags, taking into account the ambiguities inherent in these texts. We introduce a novel neural network architecture, the set-valued transformer, which can forecast sets of POS tags to provide reliable annotations for these texts. Our approach demonstrates the effectiveness of this method on a collection of 18th century French texts, as well as on a collection of early 20th century German texts, leading to significant improvements over single-tag models and leading to a high degree of accuracy when applied to an unpublished collection of German texts from the Vienna Institute of Digital Scholarship. Overall, the results show that the use of set-valued forecasting is well-suited for the task of POS labeling in historical collections. Code and data for the study can be found on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/andrewkroh/set-valued-fn. This research utilizes the dependency parsing library Allennlp and can be run with the following command: `python run_set_valued_fn.py -f path/to/model -d path/to/data -o output_file` where `output_file` will contain the reliable annotations generated by the model. Further analysis and results can be found in the directory `results/pos_set_valued_fns/`. We recommend using the Jupyter notebook to run the analysis and results, accessible via `results/pos_set_valued_fns_analysis.ipynb`. We also provide a demonstration of the model in action, available at: https://andrewkroh.github.io/set-valued-pos-demonstration/. We have also made available a collection of 18th century French texts, pre-annotated by the model, available at: https://andrewkroh.github.io/set-valued-pos-dataset/. We have also developed a novel dependency parsing task, the set-valued dependency parsing task, available at: https://andrewkroh.github.io/set-valued-dep-parsing/, along with a study of its results and analysis, available at: https://andrewkroh.github.io/set-valued-dep-parsing-results

Deep Neural Network training can be viewed as a process of solving a function optimization problem, where one is searching for the best parameter values to achieve target output results. Conventionally, this optimization process is seen as fine-tuning pre-existing network architecture features already designed to capture essential image characteristics. However, this study presents a theory that suggests these design features can be derived from the underlying image data properties through an orderly process called "layer by layer" integration. Our study offers two non-smooth cases of this integration process: one based on the principle of margin preservation, used in the development of decision trees, and the other, a more complex "diagonal" margin preservation approach, similar to recent neural network designs. For both cases, we were able to mathematically demonstrate the existence of an ordered process to derive optimal network features from image data properties. Our study also provides initial evidence of the strength of this integration process in the context of decision trees, where margin preservation has been shown to lead to over-simplified class prediction models. Our study further presents initial results suggesting that more complex "diagonal" margin preservation may offer improved performance and better data representation for further exploration. Finally, our study offers a theoretical foundation for the development of new neural network architectures with potential for improved performance and better understanding of the underlying data properties. Our study is available in its entirety on the arXiv server at a related link. For the sake of clarity and precision, our study has been divided into two parts: the first is a more theoretical contribution on the margin-based integration process, while the second is a more experimental contribution on the exploration of the "diagonal" margin preservation. Due to the limitations of arXiv's formatting constraints, our study has been further divided into two separate submissions, both of which are presented below. Submission ID: 2103.09527 (Theoretical contribution on margin-based integration process), and Submission ID: 2103.09528 (Experimental contribution on "diagonal" margin preservation).  The present submission is based on the latter, an experimental contribution on "diagonal" margin preservation.  The related theoretical contribution on margin-based integration process is presented in arXiv's submission ID: 2103.09527. We introduce an family of symmetric functions, denoted as $\mathsf{DSF}_n(q)$, derived from standard q-rook theory's combinatorial framework. These functions can be represented as weighted sums of partitions where the partition's top row does not exceed $n$, and the total number of parts does not surpass $n$, with each such partition emerging from the application of $q$-rook rules in $n \times n$ grids with specific obstacles. By interpreting $\mathsf{DSF}_n(q)$ as a limit of $q$-partitions in large square grids with particular shapes, we establish a connection to Dyck trails of length $2n$, thereby expressing $\mathsf{DSF}_n(q)$ as a sum of colored versions of Dyck trail-related symmetric functions, labeled $\mathsf{Dil}_\mu$ and $\mathsf{Dp}_\mu$ for paths with ladder-like structures $\mu$. Additionally, we demonstrate that $\mathsf{DSF}_n(q)$ can be further expressed as a $Q$-series expansion, equivalent to a modified version of Garsia-Remmel's $\mathsf{T}_n(q)$, which describes colored shuffle partitions. By examining $\mathsf{DSF}_n(1)$, we identify its underlying combinatorial structure as path-structured ribbon poset partitions, thereby providing a combinatorial interpretation of Stanley's $q$-ribbon function. Lastly, due to $\mathsf{DSF}_n(q)$'s complex nature, some aspects of this function remain yet to be fully understood and explored. Several open problems and future research directions are proposed in the concluding section. We aim to develop a novel conditional generation model that creates a seamless, never-ending single-view scene from any given image. This task is crucial for immersive experiences like VR and AR, as well as reducing visual artifacts in video transmission. Prior studies have tackled the problem using traditional generative models but achieved only partial success due to their limited capacity to capture the complex, high-fidelity scene structure. In contrast, recent conditional diffusion models excel in generating high-quality, detailed images and modeling high-entropy distributions. Building on this success, we introduce DiffDreamer, a state-of-the-art conditional diffusion model that produces realistic, endless single-views from given images. By leveraging a comprehensive dataset of 1 million images, we demonstrate DiffDreamer's ability to create realistic, infinite single-views with enhanced visual details and coherent composition. In our evaluation, it outperforms existing approaches in PSNR, SSIM, and FID scores, showcasing its superior performance and reliability. Further implementation details, including the source code and model weights, are available on our project website. Through user studies, we found that users prefer the images produced by DiffDreamer over those generated by DreamView. This model also surpasses other baselines in our internal development phase. In a critical reliability test, we discovered that models developed on larger datasets can produce high-quality images even when given only a few pixels as input. This property makes them particularly useful in applications where only a single pixel is available. Overall, our research highlights the potential of conditional diffusion models in creating seamless, never-ending single-views, outperforming existing solutions in image quality, structure, and robustness. Deep Belief Networks are widely recognized for their ability to learn independent, high-level feature sets in a self-directed manner.  However, research evidence suggests that combining multiple DBN layers into a single, Multi-layered Mixture of DBNs (MIMO) leads to enhanced accuracy.  While prior studies of MIMO architectures have focused on initial implementations where units within the same layer interact only through the model's modelled probability distribution, our research indicates that allowing interactions between units within the same layer can significantly improve performance.  We propose a novel approach, where interactions between units are introduced through a Gaussian message passing mechanism, enabling them to share features directly.  Our results demonstrate that this modification leads to high accuracy and improved robustness in a variety of scenarios, including both binary and real-valued observations.  We also present a theoretical explanation for this improvement, showing that allowing interactions between units allows redundant information to be eliminated and allowing the sharing of common features.  We test our approach on multiple prior MIMO architectures, as well as prior DBN and Autoencoder architectures, and verify that our approach leads to a general improvement in performance across a range of scenarios.  We also provide a theoretical explanation for this improvement, showing that allowing interactions between units allows redundant information to be eliminated and allowing the sharing of common features. The effectiveness of a compensation method for an industrial robot's position flatness is demonstrated. Although modern robots are designed with position feedback, their lack of internal flatness means that errors can persist due to factors like dynamic coupling and mechanical imperfections. To improve position accuracy, a novel control strategy incorporates additional sensors beyond standard feedback. With these extra data points, position tracking becomes more precise and consistent, capable of keeping pace with rapidly changing demands. Simulation and analysis reveal the benefits of this approach, showing improved two-doornail tolerance and robust tracking performance, especially in scenarios involving rapid changes. Furthermore, this flatness-based method exhibits resilient behavior in the face of model inaccuracies, making it well-suited for adaptive applications. Notably, this solution does not require adjustments even when adapting the robot's parameters for new applications, ensuring adaptability without compromising position accuracy. Moreover, this strategy shows promise for application to other positioning systems as well, suggesting a range of potential uses. Overall, this novel control strategy offers enhanced performance capabilities, making it a valuable tool for high-precision tasks. Additional research is recommended to explore integrating this method with more sophisticated estimation techniques for further optimization. A novel approach to analyzing numerous time-to-event data is presented, focusing on the dynamic relationships between past health events and future risks of new events. To be more informative, time-to-event information is considered in multiple dimensions, incorporating both the timing and number of occurrences across different health categories. To this end, a new evaluation method is developed to assess individuals' probabilities of future time-to-event occurrences at different intensity levels in various disease domains. To model these probabilities, a hierarchical framework is introduced, consisting of a global Gaussian process regression for latent life courses and local mixed models for event risks. Our proposed approach is applied to a large study of cardiovascular disease using simulated data and real observations from 8,116 patients with a previous myocardial infarction, providing new insights into how past health events relate to future risks, such as the reduced likelihood of subsequent myocardial infarctions among individuals who have experienced stroke. These results demonstrate the practical value of analyzing numerous time-to-event data in multiple states of health to better understand the complex relationships between different health events. Moreover, this approach can be used as a decision-making tool to help clinicians and patients evaluate treatment options and identify areas of high risk that require closer monitoring. Furthermore, this framework can be applied to a wide range of scientific inquiry and healthcare scenarios, such as evaluating the effectiveness of new treatments and developing personalized prevention and monitoring strategies. With the rapid growth of electronic health records and machine learning capabilities, this type of multidimensional time-to-event analysis has the potential to revolutionize the understanding and application of life course epidemiology and health informatics. To facilitate adoption, a comprehensive software package is provided for creating the type of dynamic life course health pathways and latent life course diagrams presented here, facilitating communication among researchers, clinicians, and patients. We introduce a novel quadrature approach that efficiently handles molecular continuum problems with multiple sites in contrast to traditional methods. This proposed approach is based on the Galerkin formulation and is suitable for arbitrary finite element subdomains. Furthermore, it establishes accurate integration rules for matrices involving the Laplacian and inverse Laplacian operators. This method's benefits include reduced computational complexity, simpler data structures, and faster implementation, while maintaining the same level of precision as other methods. We validate this approach by applying it to various numerical examples, including a benchmark test of the Green's function in two dimensions and a range of boundary value problems that demonstrate its robustness and efficiency. These examples include solving boundary value problems for Laplace and inverse Laplacian equations as well as a dynamic transport problem on a complex domain with multiple sites. However, the quality of DL predictions heavily relies on the accuracy and sufficiency of training data, which often contains flaws. Label noise is a common issue in medical datasets, resulting from various errors such as misdiagnosed patients, incorrect chart information, and annotation mistakes. Currently, there is no standard solution to address label noise, and most existing methods focus on modeling noise distribution or using robust optimization for model training. In this paper, we take a different approach by addressing label noise through correcting inaccurate labels. We propose a novel mechanism called the Bayesian Analytics Guided Label Restoration (BGLR) method, which aims to find the underlying, noise-free labels. By integrating Bayesian analytics principles, we develop a mechanism to temporarily remove images from the training data and subsequently re-introduce them for further analysis, allowing us to determine which labels are corrupted and correct them. The BGLR method is able to provide noise-free labels without relying on secondary datasets or complex mathematical formulations. To address this issue, we propose an alternative method that incorporates timed definitions to enhance postcondition expressions in HOL.  By allowing the specification of time limits for operations, this approach enables the definition of functions with bounded processing times, effectively simulating an environment with limited computational capacity.  This technique effectively creates a scenario where functions are operated on as if they were part of a limited computational environment, even within the context of HOL's unrestricted mathematical framework.  By demonstrating the applicability of timed definitions to various domains, including data structures, network protocols, and abstract interpretation, we have effectively expanded the scope of preconditions and postconditions in HOL, allowing for more precise and realistic modeling of functions. We introduce a modified Skyrme model incorporating a Born-Infeld term, coupled with a massless $U(1)$ gauge field. For this new model, we derive classical equations of motion, impose duality transformations, and identify conditions for self-dual equations. Furthermore, we prove the non-rigidity of the resulting Born-Infeld Skyrme model, demonstrate its separation into decoupled equations, describe solutions representing plane waves and linearly propagating oscillating waves, and finally, discuss the emergence of gauge field oscillations in the far distant region. Additionally, we explore infant Skyrme models with non-Abelian and Chern-Simons terms. For these extended models, we establish equations of topological charge and derive self-dual equations, representing new self-dual solitons. We also discuss the far distant behavior of gauge fields in these scenarios. In the non-Abelian case, we obtain two separate equations for the SU(2) gauge field, and demonstrate its separation into decoupled equations. For the Chern-Simons case, we prove the non-rigidity of the infant Skyrme model, and identify conditions for self-dual equations involving the CS term vanishing. Our work provides a foundation for further research on these extended models. We hope that our study will inspire the development of more advanced mathematical models. Deep learning models are highly effective due to their ability to recognize patterns in data. However, their applications are limited by the availability of specialized models for specific tasks. To overcome this limitation, researchers have developed data enhancement techniques that utilize the knowledge embedded in models to create new, artificially diverse training examples. These techniques facilitate the transfer of model knowledge to diverse areas, enabling the creation of general specialist models from a limited set of training examples. In this paper, we explore various data enhancement techniques and evaluate their performance on specific tasks, including generating code and creating dataset cards. Our experiments demonstrate that a semi-supervised approach yielding significant improvements in model performance after data enhancement, with average increases in F1-score and METEOR metric ranging from 10-40%. Notably, the semi-supervised approach outperforms a supervised method in generating code. While our results reveal that data enhancement can be an effective means of leveraging model knowledge, the choice of method and parameters depends on the specific task and dataset. Moreover, the accuracy of data enhancement methods directly impacts model performance, with more accurate generated examples resulting in better performance. To promote transparency and understanding in GPT-like models, we also propose creating "explanatory" data enhancement examples that can significantly improve model performance, even when the model has not seen similar examples during training. Our proposed method has the potential to expand the applicability of large language models, enabling the creation of general specialist models for various application domains. To support model development, we have released our code, dataset cards, and data generation challenge on GitHub. Furthermore, the paper includes additional experimental results, including model performance on specific tasks, as well as relevant figures and tables. Finally, related work is outlined in a separate document. The generated data, data distribution plots, and human evaluation results can be accessed via the following GitHub links: https://github.com/asharakeh/generative-data-enhancement and https://github.com/asharakeh/data-environment. The paper builds upon a prior version, https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.11243, with significant methodological improvements and novel data enhancement approaches. The key differences between the two papers lie in their focus, with the prior version exploring the impact of data enhancement on programming languages, whereas this version delves into the role of data augmentation in transforming the data environment. Moreover, the current paper incorporates new data augmentation methods and evaluates model performance across a broader range of tasks, including generating code and creating dataset cards. Measuring the production of two Higgs bosons ($HH$) in association with a vector boson ($V$) is crucial for examining Higgs potential instability and testing Higgs particle interactions. Simulations predict $VHH$ production to be less frequent than dominant $Ht$ and $HW$ processes, yet it can be detected with higher selectivity due to a lower background likelihood of $t\bar{t}$ and vector boson exclusive production. This research aims to investigate the identification of $HH$ and $VH$ production using proton-proton collision data collected by the ATLAS detector at 13 TeV in 2015-2018, totaling 361 pb$^{-1}$ of integrated luminosity. By simulating different $V$ production scenarios, including both $W$ and $Z$, the analysis aims to detect $VHH$ signals with statistical significance greater than 5 standard deviations, by comparing them to observed data. These results will serve as a foundation for refining this detection method to identify $VHH$ signals with increased certainty in future analyses. Once fully developed, this analysis is expected to be able to detect $VHH$ signals with statistical significance greater than 5 and 4 standard deviations for $W$ and $Z$ vector bosons, respectively, assuming $H$ production cross-sections consistent with the Standard Model. Even in the absence of $VHH$ signals, the analysis will have a likelihood rejection factor of 0.25 for $t\bar{t}$ and $HW$ backgrounds against $VHH$ signals, thereby enabling this detection method to be used to measure $VHH$ signals with increased certainty in future analyses. This rejection factor is expected to remain consistent even if $V$ vector bosons change to $t$ or $W$ vector bosons. Moreover, the analysis will have a likelihood rejection factor of 0.5 for $Z$ vector bosons against $VHH$ signals, thereby enabling this detection method to be used to measure $VHH$ signals with increased certainty in future analyses. Finally, the analysis will have a likelihood rejection factor of 0.5 for $t$ vector bosons against $VHH$ signals, thereby enabling this detection method to be used to measure $VHH$ signals with increased certainty in future analyses. The results of this research will contribute significantly to ongoing efforts to detect $VHH$ signals with increased certainty. The method proposed here will serve as the foundation for refining this detection method

The spin maser, a highly sensitive device, detects minute magnetic field fluctuations near the Earth's core, crucial for seismology and Earth core magnetometry. We've developed an advanced digital technology that enables the construction of a more sensitive alkaline spin maser. The system consists of a 0.1 Torr chamber containing 100 milliliters of liquid potassium tetraborate and a superconducting magnet providing a 12 Gauss magnetic field. The temperature is maintained at 3.5 Kelvin by a helium-3 refrigerator. The maser signal is digitized at 40 million samples per second and processed digitally to enhance sensitivity. The system's sensitivity is currently limited by noise in the laboratory environment. Ideal conditions could yield a signal-to-noise ratio improvement of about 10 times over existing analog systems. Our digital technology holds promise for significant advancements in various alkaline spin masers. The system is completely automated, allowing for unattended operation for extended periods. The digital signal processing techniques employed can be applied to enhance sensitivity in other maser types. The system's source code and hardware designs are available for free, potentially enabling the construction of a sensitive spin maser by any researcher. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of digital technology in advancing research tools, providing a new path for scientific instrument development. The cost of building a digital alkaline spin maser is comparable to that of a digital ion trap, approximately $200,000. The system's digital signal processing employs a sophisticated algorithm designed to extract the maser signal, suppressing noise. In recent times, investigations into dark energy and dark matter have dominated research into fundamental physics due to their profound influence on the universe's evolution. Research into neutralinos as potential sources of dark matter and dark energy is presented in this paper. If a supersymmetry theory is realized, the lightest neutralino is likely to be the first candidate for dark matter. In the context of the universe's late-stage evolution, a neutralino's mass increase could result from a D-terms contribution, potentially making it a candidate for dark energy as well. Using a neutralino model with this property, the interaction between neutralinos and gamma rays can be examined. In specific cases, the neutralino's decay into photinos and gauginos may produce gamma-ray spectra characterized by features at high energy, while other scenarios may yield continuous spectra. By analyzing these possibilities, constraints on the neutralino's mass range where its dark matter and dark energy potential is valid can be established. The primary goal of the NLP4SL task was to evaluate the capacity of neural models to learn precise, complex word meanings from the context of Zhihu paper titles originating from Chinese language sources, utilizing a simplified self-supervised approach with several key elements. The process began with a pre-trained, token-level model fine-tuned for out-of-distribution context prediction tasks, incorporating a specialized token-type system to distinguish between individual characters and words within each context. The model also leveraged character-based word representations and explicitly defined token sets to prevent word degradation during training. The resulting model effectively identified 94.71% of single-word challenges from the NLP4SL dataset without relying on an external dictionary. The process involved deriving complex word meanings from single characters through statistical analysis, in addition to a collection of defined character definitions. The model also demonstrated an ability to recognize character-level challenges, achieving a 94.05% accuracy in identifying single-character challenges without a dictionary. The full implementation details and associated code are publicly accessible via the link: https://github.com/whwu/SL4NLP. The model's performance was also enhanced through the incorporation of multiple training objectives, including three key components: a character-based objective to capture character-level meaning, a word-based objective to preserve word-level integrity, and a type-based objective to promote the use of a defined token set. The model's performance was evaluated using a 5-fold cross-validation strategy. The detailed findings and implementation guidance are presented in this abstract, with the goal of inspiring future research and promoting the development of more robust, out-of-vocabulary word representations. This research introduces a advanced predictive method known as adaptive spectral Koopman technique, rooted in the standard spectral Koopman method. The latter uses spectral decomposition to model the behavior of complex dynamical systems, specifically those that cannot be solved with classical methods. However, traditional Koopman methods have limitations, mainly due to the requirement for a large, typically low-rank matrix collection. To overcome this, the adaptive spectral Koopman method projects this matrix collection onto a lower-dimensional, multi-dimensional grid structure, preserving its low dimensionality throughout. By doing so, it enables the efficient modeling and prediction of highly complex systems within a relatively small space. The method's foundation is rooted in the theory that the rich dynamics of a high-dimensional system can often be captured by a small number of carefully selected points, known as extremal points. By incorporating these points and a few additional, strategically selected intermediary points, the adaptive spectral Koopman method can accurately predict a system's behavior, even when the underlying causes remain unknown. Furthermore, the method's adaptive nature allows it to continuously monitor and adjust its performance, ensuring optimal results. To validate its effectiveness, the adaptive spectral Koopman method was tested on a series of complex, chaotic systems, resulting in remarkable predictions that matched the actual behavior of the systems in every detail. By employing sparse grid techniques, the method was able to predict far beyond what was initially thought possible, offering a powerful new tool for the study and prediction of complex, high-dimensional systems. The Sinkhorn algorithm, originally designed for optimal transport, can be applied across various fields. Though it's known for converging slowly, with a sublinear rate under certain conditions, past research revealed an intriguing obstacle: a expression that, when set to zero, renders the algorithm non-convergent. While researchers found ways to circumvent this issue, its solution remains elusive. As such, analyzing the Sinkhorn method necessitates accounting for this constraint. Under specific assumptions, this study demonstrates the algorithm's convergence in various scenarios, including with a modified version that avoids the Schrödinger equation's unsolvability. Furthermore, this modification is shown to be applicable to a range of important applications, including clustering in graphs. To investigate the algorithm's performance, several numerical experiments were conducted, highlighting its effectiveness in a clustering task. In addition to this practical application, this research also explores broader theoretical implications, including the relationship between the Sinkhorn algorithm and the Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality. Ultimately, this study provides novel insights into the algorithm's performance and its potential uses in a variety of contexts. The COVID-19 pandemic has profoundly impacted urban settings worldwide, 
inducing significant changes in human behavior and circulation patterns. 
A multi-faceted analysis of urban mobility and economic activity is 
essential to grasp the scope and consequences of these alterations. 
Merging statistical examination and qualitative probes, this research 
investigates the various aspects of pandemic-induced modifications to 
mobility and circulation patterns in Santiago, Chile. A comparative 
analysis of daily and weekly urban mobility and circulation volume 
across different income groups revealed a more pronounced decline in weekly 
mobility, affecting lower-income individuals to a greater extent. 
Consequently, the disparity in urban circulation is increased following 
the pandemic, with an observed 67% higher chance of individuals from lower-
income backgrounds interacting with people from lower socioeconomic 
backgrounds compared to pre-pandemic interaction patterns. 
Notably, the pandemic not only amplified existing income disparities 
affecting urban circulation but also introduced new disparities not 
prevalent in pre-pandemic circulation patterns. 
A follow-up investigation involving qualitative interviews revealed that 
the primary factors driving these changes are pandemic-related fear and 
government-implemented restrictions, with socioeconomic status playing a 
significant role in the magnitude of these changes. 
It is crucial to recognize that the socioeconomic disparities 
disproportionately affecting urban circulation during the pandemic may not 
completely reverse once pandemic-related restrictions subside. 
Therefore, the policymakers must adopt a more nuanced approach, 
particularly considering the long-term consequences of pre- and 
post-pandemic urban circulation disparity on urban development and 
planning. 
Moreover, the research highlights the critical need for increased 
socioeconomic equality in urban circulation and may serve as a potential 
mechanism for reducing pre- and post-pandemic urban circulation disparity 
in the future. 
A potential strategy could involve the creation of 'circular segregation 
zones' where urban circulation disparity is minimized.

impact of pandemic-induced urban circulation disparity on urban

The traditional understanding of chiral optical properties has been primarily based on molecules exhibiting chirality. In contrast, this study explores the concept of chiral chamber properties, where chirality arises from three-dimensional structural geometry. To demonstrate the presence of chiral chambers in optical materials, we propose and successfully create (and later improve) thin optical chambers with broken mirror symmetry. Due to the inherent three-dimensional nature of chiral chambers, they inherently possess surface chirality. Existing map representations, however, often fail to capture the organizational structure of systems due to their focus on detailed spatial information. To address this limitation, a novel diagrammatic representation called HiTMap, implemented using Tool Command Language (TCL), is introduced. HiTMap leverages a hierarchical structure to capture a system's topology, incorporating node and edge representations that encode important spatial and organizational information. By incorporating these capabilities, HiTMap demonstrates improved performance in identifying optimal paths and distinguishing between exploration and delinquent behaviors in unfamiliar environments. By embedding unfocused and focused strategies within multi-agent Unfamiliar Environment (UE) scenarios, HiTMap's effectiveness is demonstrated through the achievement of higher rewards in both scenarios. This study investigates optimal portfolio management for time-invariant investors with a power of alpha utility function, which measures wealth relative to a benchmark. Unlike standard power utility, which assesses wealth absolutely, this relative benchmark approach offers more realistic investment models. We demonstrate that optimal portfolios can be described by a linear mean-variance model if an analytical solution to the relative power of alpha functional is found. Otherwise, a numerical approach, such as Monte Carlo simulation, is required to determine the optimal portfolio. Furthermore, we extend our model to account for short-selling restrictions and provide a numerical example to illustrate our method. Additionally, we consider a scenario where investment costs are quadratic and sublinear in wealth, which allows us to close the analytical gap and develop a closed-form solution for optimal portfolios in the absence of short-selling limitations. This solution reveals that higher values of alpha lead to more aggressive investment strategies, which are supported by both analytical and numerical results. Ultimately, we examine how the alpha parameter impacts optimal portfolios through both numerical calculations and analytical solutions. A full latent space is mapped to a sparser subspace using a differentiable transportation system, and the network is optimized using a novel loss function. Unlike existing methods, this approach does not rely on non-differentiable sparsity functions, allowing latent space points to be repelled from each other after training. In a dilute Bose gas represented by a Schrödinger field theory with small $N$-body interactions, the phase shifts for low-momentum scattering with $2N$ particles are known to be proportional to $1/(E_{F}^{2}k^{5})$ for small $k$, where $E_{F}$ is the Fermi energy derived from the gas's Fermi momentum. We investigate an ideal Bose fluid with no interactions but a similar phase shift profile through a $D$-dimensional free field theory. Despite the lack of interactions, the ideal fluid still exhibits a Pauli obstruction, a global invariance-breaking anomaly, that persists in the ideal fluid's Hilbert space. We demonstrate that this obstruction's strength is analogous to $N$ in the phase shift's $1/(E_{F}^{2}k^{5})$ proportionality. Notably, the Pauli obstruction's effect can be seen as a non-topological fractional quantum Hall state that emerges in the ideal Bose fluid when represented through a specific bosonic lattice model with $SU(N)$ symmetry. This non-Abelian state of the ideal fluid shares characteristics with a $U(1)$ spin liquid in three dimensions and a Kitaev model in lower dimensions. We further explore how to characterize the ideal Bose fluid's symmetry-breaking anomaly through unitary transformations and equivalence classes of unitary operators. Notably, the Pauli obstruction's effect cannot be fully removed by any unitary transformation, and the ideal fluid's symmetry-breaking anomaly can be characterized by a specific property within the Hilbert space. We further explore how to characterize the Pauli obstruction's effect through equivalence classes of unitary operators and show that the ideal fluid's symmetry-breaking anomaly can be fully represented and characterized by the $SU(N)$ symmetry. We developed a novel stochastic approach, stochastic tensor singular value decomposition (SSTVD), that enables the calculation of singular value factorization for tensors without exceeding available memory. This method capitalizes on parallel processing capabilities, making it highly suitable for distributed computing environments. Additionally, it can handle large-scale tensors by dividing the data into manageable chunks and processing each iteration to completion before moving on to the next. Furthermore, our approach allows for easy identification of approximate low-rank tensor structures. We demonstrate the effectiveness of SSTVD using real-world data from the fields of medicine and astronomy. We also compare the results to demonstrate that our approach can produce comparable outcomes to existing methods while reducing computational time significantly, specifically, by an order of O(n). A great number of natural and man-made phenomena can be effectively modeled as dynamic networks, which are researched in various fields by utilizing the tools from theoretical linear and nonlinear dynamical systems. Unlike the widespread use of black-box techniques in machine learning, graph embedding methods, particularly graph neural networks, explicitly incorporate the structural information into the latent space representation. This allows for the preservation of important dynamic properties in emerging graphs, which are crucial for the functioning of various systems. This paper delves into the world of evolving graphs, presenting different types and proposing a new method, EGAE, that leverages autoencoders to capture the intricate characteristics of emerging graphs. By utilizing the Multiple Set Canonical Correlation Analysis, EGAE aims to preserve topological properties, enhance connectivity, and maintain the stability of emerging graph dynamics. Our empirical findings on both artificial and real-world datasets demonstrate the superiority of EGAE over existing methods in preserving structural and visual characteristics of emerging graphs. Additionally, we showcase the efficacy of EGAE-trained models using node classification tasks. EGAE source code will be made available upon acceptance. We introduce OntoPlot, a innovative visualization concept that displays connections between entities in ontologies, including their hierarchies and relationships. Current pedestrian detection systems face challenges due to their rigid bounding boxes. These boxes struggle to enclose deformable objects, resulting in numerous false positives. Typically, these false positives are eliminated through high-complexity box pruning methods. In this research, a low-complexity box reordering technique is introduced to suppress false positives and reduce inference time, leveraging the inherent density property of pedestrians to achieve this. The method's success relies on a novel density prediction network that generates density maps for input images. The density maps are then used to derive an optimal box reordering list via the Steiner point algorithm, ensuring all positive boxes are arranged in order of decreasing density values. A subsequent ranking-based selector is designed to discard low-density boxes, boosting the model's detection precision without increasing inference time. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through experiments conducted on various datasets, showcasing its domain adaptation capabilities and superior performance compared to other box pruning techniques. The code is publicly available on GitHub. Comprehensive evaluation methods are proposed to ensure the accuracy of box reordering and performance comparison with other pruning techniques. The results indicate that the method achieves an mAP increase of 2.8% and 1.5% on Citypersons and Caltech datasets, respectively, without a significant increase in box count, while outperforming other box pruning techniques. The method also shows improved generalizability on datasets not used in training, such as the VeRiChallenge benchmark. The method's performance is comparable to other state-of-the-art pedestrian detection models, with the ability to adapt to in-domain data. The method's success lies in its ability to eliminate false positives through box reordering without relying on complex box matching techniques, making it suitable for real-time pedestrian detection applications. The method's performance is further validated through occlusion and re-identification experiments, with the ability to maintain a high detection precision even after occlusion and the ability to perform re-identification at a high precision. The method's performance is documented through two videos demonstrating the method's performance on the VeRiChallenge benchmark. The method's performance is also demonstrated through domain adaptation experiments conducted on Citypersons and Caltech datasets, with the ability to adapt the method to out-of-domain data. The method's performance is further evaluated through eye-tracking and attention analysis, with the ability to analyze the method's attention and perform eye-tracking. The method's performance is also demonstrated through box reordering experiments conducted on other datasets, with the ability to improve the method's performance on other datasets, such as MS COCO and ImageNet.

This is achieved through two high-performance calculation methods, one of which is based on density functional theory and the other on grain surface potential calculations. In our quest to harness the power of quantum computers, it's crucial that our quantum states can efficiently be measured and exploited for practical purposes. By projecting a quantum state onto specific target states, we gain valuable information about the state's characteristics. However, current methods to estimate projection outcomes between general quantum states and axes (specifically, 2D Shannon shades) are too resource-intensive, necessitating high-depth quantum circuits. Here, we introduce a set of low-depth, randomly constructed quantum circuits, dubbed low-depth RQC (LDRQC), which can efficiently rotate Shannon shades. These circuits achieve this rotation with a significantly reduced number of gates, comparable to the depth of quantum simulations. We've further adapted these circuits to rotate more complex, multi-dimensional 'polyshades', allowing for the estimation of their projection outcomes with relative low computational costs. Our findings suggest polyshades offer improved trade-offs between state complexity and projection overlap compared to Shannon shades. Moreover, we've discovered polyshades with a limited number of unique projection outcomes, known as 'decision polyshades', which can efficiently approximate polyshades and enhance the accuracy of their projection estimates. Our work presents a new set of tools for quantum state processing, complementing existing methods like quantum Hamiltonian learning. By leveraging these tools, researchers can design novel quantum information applications, such as decision-based algorithms, which utilize decision polyshades to answer specific questions about general quantum states. We've proposed a simple protocol for this task and demonstrated its efficiency, showcasing its potential as a valuable addition to the quantum information processing toolkit. We've also introduced a new set of questions related to general quantum information, which can be easily answered using decision polyshades, offering a practical application of quantum information principles. We conclude by speculating on the potential connections between polyshades, quantum information, and decision theory. Our findings suggest that polyshades, with their decision properties, may serve as a fundamental unit of quantum information, similar to qubits. We propose further investigation into polyshades and their potential role in quantum information theory. The code used in this research is available upon request. Furthermore, we've identified areas for potential improvements, such as exploring low-depth RQC variants that preserve specific target state properties (e.g., equidistant states) without requiring extensive quantum circuits. This could lead to the development of more efficient quantum algorithms that take advantage of these equidistant properties. Moreover, our research has implications for the design of quantum information protocols, which may be adapted to utilize specific target state properties

Utilizing large pre-trained transformer models (e.g. BERT) in multilingual settings has shown to deliver high performance, but their large size makes them impractical for mobile and embedded devices. Knowledge distillation allows a smaller language model to learn from a larger, pre-trained model's outputs, making it accessible to devices with limited resources. Previous studies have explored the robustness of this process under various conditions, yet the basic training objective remains unclear. In our research, we investigate the training objective's role in knowledge transfer between large and small models. We discovered that distillation's initial objective can be replaced with a simple quantization operation without compromising the model's translation quality. This unexpected result raises questions about the necessity of distillation and suggests that it could be used as an efficiency tool instead. We evaluated multiple quantization and distillation methods, comparing their performance in reducing model size while maintaining translation quality on low resource MT tasks. Too Fragile To Handle presents our findings, providing a comprehensive analysis of each method's adaptability when training a small model to mimic a large target model's behavior under various conditions. We investigated the impact of several key hyperparameters, including learning rate, teacher-student similarity, and unsupervised cross entropy. Our results show that distillation can be an effective tool for reducing model size, but may not be necessary depending on the approach and hyperparameters used. Ultimately, our research provides a clearer understanding of the knowledge transfer process and identifies areas for further investigation. The goal of Image Description is to generate detailed and natural-sounding descriptions 
for given images based on the understanding of visual elements and their relationships.
Notably, the current top-performing models exhibit significant shortfalls in their descriptions 
where crucial details are missing or superfluous information is included. To address these 
shortfalls, we introduce the Prompt Image Description task and propose the PIDS task, 
where images are paired with initial prompts and the task involves generating detailed and 
natural-sounding descriptions that incorporate these prompts. By utilizing pre-initialized 
CLIP models, our proposed framework can produce high-quality descriptions while maintaining 
its robustness and keeping model weights under manageable size. To support our proposal, 
we establish the PIDS dataset consisting of a large collection of image-description pairs along 
with prompts derived from extensive human labelling. Our experiments confirm that our model 
achieves better results compared to traditional image description tasks, and we provide 
further analysis on the characteristics of prompt-driven descriptions. Our code and dataset are 
available for public access on GitHub.

The concept of damage in this context is often associated with harm, for example physical or emotional suffering, that is easily identifiable and understandable. However, the broader and more complex nature of damage has not been adequately explored, particularly in how it is caused. By applying causal analysis to damage, this study aims to develop a more comprehensive and rigorous definition, thereby facilitating the creation of better-intentioned consequentialist AI systems. To achieve this, the study undertakes a causal examination of damage, which involves identifying the specific forms damage can take and the mechanisms by which they are caused. Our findings suggest that damage can manifest as positive or negative physical, psychological, or social changes, resulting from actions driven by intentions, consequences, or social obligations. Moreover, the mechanisms causing damage in consequentialist agents are often rooted in the social model of agency, which highlights issues like transparency, communication, and autonomy problems. By shedding light on these underlying mechanisms, the study provides valuable insights for designers and regulators of consequentialist AI systems, while also highlighting potential solutions to minimize damage caused to individuals and society as a whole. Ultimately, the study's key contributions lie in its definition of damage, its causal analysis, and its social model of agency, which collectively provide a foundation for further research in this area. The study's primary limitation is its reliance on pre-existing definitions of harm and social models of agency, which are not exhaustively explored in this study. Can we extend the definition of damage and the social model of agency to create better-consequentialist AI systems? Can we design and regulate consequentialist AI systems to minimize damage caused to individuals and society? Can we define new definitions of damage and the social model of agency for specific applications (e.g., physical vs. psychological damage)? We propose Zero-shot Voice Interpretation, a task that enables voice-enabled systems to convey meaning without requiring extensive training on numerous categories. Our approach involves transforming audio inputs into text-based representations, then mapping these to concepts, and finally generating descriptions based on selected concepts. To tackle this newly identified task, we developed a versatile model framework that can be used across multiple datasets and benchmarks, allowing for the analysis of both automatic and human evaluation metrics. Our model achieved top results on automatic evaluation on Soloud, a dataset that facilitates zero-shot reasoning, and demonstrated strong performance on human evaluation across three datasets: Emotion Recognition, a two-class category task, and two multi-class categories: US Air Quality and Product Reviews, both requiring zero-shot generalization. Our model's performance opens up new possibilities for semantic descriptions of spoken words and conversations, paving the way for future advancements. Notably, our work received top scores in the Zero-shot Voice Interpretation track of the Intent City Challenge 2022. Breast cancer is a major threat to women's health, and the COVID-19 pandemic has introduced a new risk factor that needs to be carefully studied.  Radiotherapy planning requires accurate segmentation of COVID-19 lesions to ensure patients receive the correct treatment, but this process can be time-consuming and labor-intensive for radiologists.  Due to the scarcity of data and poor visibility of COVID-19 lesions on mammograms, developing accurate automatic segmentation has been a significant challenge.  We propose a new deep learning approach, called WW-Net, which is designed to accurately identify and segment COVID-19 lesions in mammograms without the need for manual segmentation.  WW-Net uses a unique combination of weakly supervised learning techniques, including distillation and multi-task training, to locate and extract COVID-19 lesions in images.  By leveraging annotation from multiple sources, including image-level and pixel-level information, WW-Net is able to improve its performance and reduce the impact of limited data.  We evaluated WW-Net on a dataset of 800 mammograms and found that it outperforms state-of-the-art segmentation techniques by a significant margin, with an average Dice score of 0.65 and Average Absolute Error of 0.095.  Additionally, we found that the distillation component of WW-Net improves its performance by up to 9% in terms of Dice score and 15% in terms of Average Absolute Error.  Overall, our approach demonstrates the potential to accurately identify and segment COVID-19 lesions in mammograms, which could lead to improved diagnosis and treatment for women with the disease.  In particular, we found that the proposed method can be used to automatically create high-quality segmentations from minimal annotations, which could help to expand the availability of data for training and validation.  Furthermore, our approach outperforms state-of-the-art segmentation techniques on average by a significant margin, which could help to improve the accuracy of breast cancer diagnosis during the pandemic. Detecting vertebrae in the human spine is an essential yet complex step in vertebral fracture diagnosis through CT scans. Due to the curved and twisted nature of the spine, positioning challenges are often encountered. Current vertebrae recognition methods rely heavily on external regulation, which often leads to inaccuracies in positioning, resulting in failure to identify vertebrae or incorrect matches. To address these limitations, a novel approach has been developed that combines spine rectification and anatomically constrained enhancement. By projecting a straight line onto the CT image, the position of the vertebrae column is localized. Vertebral body corners are then identified and connected to form a rectified spine profile, which serves as a reference point for positioning. Each vertebra is positioned by matching template slices to the query slice based on the characteristics of the vertebral body. To prevent external influences, positioning results are subjected to anatomically constrained enhancement, which incorporates characteristics from adjacent vertebras to improve recognition accuracy. To calculate the distance between vertebrae, a template-based approach is used to measure the height and spacing of vertebral bodies. Our approach has been evaluated using two public CT datasets, demonstrating superior performance compared to current state-of-the-art methods, with an average recognition rate of 98.35% and height/spacing recognition rate of 97.95% for dataset1 and 98.65% + 97.55% for dataset2 at optimal parameter settings. Moreover, it significantly outperformed recent methods, with a substantial recognition rate increase of at least 2% for dataset1 and 4% for dataset2. To the best of our knowledge, this approach has not been previously documented in the literature. To facilitate adoption, the source code is available for academic purposes at https://github.com/whuwenqi/Spine-Rectification-AcE. Our model has also demonstrated excellent performance across different CT datasets and vertebra types, as shown in the supplementary results. Evaluating the depth in light field images is crucial for various applications like virtual reality, robotics, and image enhancement. We introduce an innovative, efficient method for depth estimation in light field images that leverages convolutional neural networks and incorporates occlusion awareness. Our approach utilizes a novel architecture, the Occlusion-Responsive Expense Creator, which dynamically assigns weights to each image slice based on expected contribution to depth estimation, considering potential occlusions. Results from extensive experiments highlight the significance of accounting for occlusions and demonstrate the superior performance of our method compared to established benchmarks. Our study also explores the impact of distinct occlusion scenarios on the performance of our approach. Our code and methodology are publicly available on GitHub. Experiment outcomes show that our proposed technique outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of overall depth estimation accuracy. Specifically, our method exhibits a notable improvement, with 0.96 $\pm$ 0.10 m AE in convergence of 10% occlusion and 0.85 $\pm$ 0.10 m AE in convergence of 20% occlusion, when compared to other methods. Even in scenarios with minimal occlusions (0% and 10%), our method shows comparable performance with small improvements over existing methods. When applied to datasets with extreme occlusions like "bug" and "car", our approach outperforms other methods by a significant margin.
